name: Hydroquinone bleaching creams (1920s)

lead: Hydroquinone is a skin-lightening agent that became the main active ingredient in bleaching creams after mercury-based products were restricted. People used these creams to lighten the skin and even out dark spots and uneven pigmentation.

The lightening effect of hydroquinone was first reported in 1936, and early twentieth-century bleaches were mostly ammoniated mercury creams marketed as freckle removers and skin bleaches. Dermatology reports from the 1970s and 1980s documented a pigmentation disorder, exogenous ochronosis, after long use of strong hydroquinone creams.

paras: The creams were applied to the skin, often daily, over weeks to months. Case series from South Africa describe use over a few years with thorough rubbing in and sun exposure before ochronosis developed. Hydroquinone is now generally sold or prescribed at regulated strengths in many countries.

Case reports and series describe blue-black discolouration and colloid milium after long-term use of strong hydroquinone creams. The US FDA revoked its earlier approval of OTC hydroquinone in 2006 and banned it in 2020, and in EU member states it is prescription-only.

chain: Skin and dark spots lighten over weeks
angle.text: The creams were applied topically to lighten overall skin tone or fade hyperpigmentation. Hydroquinone is still described as one of the most effective treatments for hyperpigmentation under supervised use.

lead: Hydroquinone bleaching creams are skin-lightening creams that use hydroquinone, a compound that reduces pigment, to lighten the skin and fade dark patches.[1] Hydroquinone's skin-lightening effect was first reported in 1936, and it later replaced ammoniated mercury, which had been the main ingredient in early twentieth-century creams sold as freckle removers and skin bleaches.[1][2]

People used the creams to achieve a lighter or more even complexion. Mass-produced lightening creams were among the most popular cosmetics worldwide by the twentieth century, bought by white, Black and brown women alike; in the 1920s and 1930s many white consumers turned to tanning lotions instead.[2]

Dermatology literature from the mid-1970s to the 1980s reported exogenous ochronosis and colloid milium after prolonged use of strong hydroquinone creams, including a series of thirty-five cases in South Africa and reports in American Black patients using 2 percent creams.[3][4] These reports are the main reason the creams appear in historical accounts of skin lightening harms.
infobox: OTC banned in US (2020); Rx-only in EU

paras: Early twentieth-century lightening creams relied mainly on ammoniated mercury, which pharmaceutical texts recommended for skin infections and dark spots while also warning of its harms.[2] Mercury was restricted by the US in 1973, South Africa in 1975 and the European Economic Community in 1976, and hydroquinone became the main replacement.[2]

Hydroquinone's lightening effect was first reported in 1936; it appeared in a sunscreen in the 1950s where lightening was an unintended effect, and was trialled for hyperpigmentation in 1961.[1] In 1982 the US FDA classified it as generally recognised as safe and effective; the FDA revoked that approval in 2006 and banned OTC hydroquinone in 2020.[1]

A 1975 report described an outbreak of ochronosis and colloid milium after use of strong hydroquinone creams, developing only after a few years and when sun exposure and thorough rubbing-in were present; it covered thirty-five cases in South Africa.[3] A 1985 report described two American Black patients who developed pitch-black pigmentation and colloid milium after using 2 percent hydroquinone creams, which it noted were among the first such cases outside Africa.[4]
Exogenous ochronosis has also been reported after topical phenol, and after oral or injected antimalarials.[5][6]
Published human data on these creams consist chiefly of case reports and case series on ochronosis rather than trials of cosmetic efficacy.[3][4]

timeline.event: Hydroquinone's skin-lightening effect is first reported.[1]
